1         Function description
                   A system that automatically determines and provides lists of frequencies that are
                   available for use in 6 GHz band.

                   As of now, AFC task is confined to country code US and Region FCC.




1.1                Introduction

      •   AFC is Required for Registration of Standard Power Devices (SPDs) with AFC Systems,
          Operation of AFC Systems in the 6 GHz Environment, creation of Test and Certification
          Procedures for the Band Ecosystem.
      •   AFC device send request to AFC System(Server) . The AFC System can determine Available
          Spectrum based on PSD across a range of frequencies, or based on EIRP for a list of Channels,
          or both.
      •   AFC proposed 6 GHz band for standard-power unlicensed devices to avoid interference with
          incumbent users.
      •   AFC Create standards which comport to regulatory requirements provided by the FCC and the
          US Code of Federal Regulations.
      •   AFC System Determination of Available Frequencies and Maximum Permissible Power as
          Communicated to the SPD Device Upon Registration and Request.

1.2              Security

TLS establishment includes Server Certificate Validation
• Assumed AFC device is securely configured with trust basis
• AFC server’s URL
• CA root certificate
The AFC Device validates the server certificate and does not connect if validation fails
• strict match against hostname in AFC URL
• validate certificate chain to configured CA root certificate
• certificate revocation status (e.g. using OCSP stapling)
• Protects against inadvertent connection to “rogue” AFC servers
TLS ciphers ensure strong encryption and integrity protection

1         Introduction
    Airtime Management (ATM) includes Airtime Fairness (ATF), Weighted Airtime Fairness (WATF),
Airtime Control (ATC) and Throughput Control (TPC).

1.1                Introduction to ATF

❑ ATF means “Airtime Fairness”.
❑ Station airtime fairness works in the same WMM AC in a group by using DWRR.
         To make all stations have the same airtime usage in the same WMM AC.
         To avoid that the slow client use too much airtime and decrease the total throughput.
❑ In other words, we change station’s Tx packet schedule to achieve airtime fairness among stations.

1.2                Introduction to WATF

❑ ATF means “Weighted Airtime Fairness”.
❑ We divide Stations into 4 groups. In different group, we give the different airtime quantum.
         Level 0 – airtime quantum is 1ms.
         Level 1 – airtime quantum is 2ms.
         Level 2 – airtime quantum is 3ms.

         Level 3 – airtime quantum is 4ms.
❑ In WATF mode, we can service VIP station by setting it in high level group.
❑ The lowest level group can be use to “guest station”.
❑ If you don’t set MAC address in any level, we will use Level 0’s airtime quantum by default.

1.3                Introduction to ATC & TPC

❑ Use the “Group round robin”
❑ Airtime ratio control by group

❑ Bandwidth(Throughput) control by group
         Guarantee the min throughput
         Limit the max throughput

1         Introduction
MU-MIMO (Multi-User MIMO) is a technique by which multiple stations (STAs), each with one or more
antennas, either simultaneously transmit to a single STA or simultaneously receive from a single STA
independent data streams over the same radio frequencies.

1.1                 Introduction to Downlink MU-MIMO (DL MU-MIMO)

❑ Downlink MU-MIMO is a technology based on Explicit Transmit Beamforming.




❑ Explicit Transmit Beamforming (eTxBF)
      •   A transmitter signaling with focus energy to a receiver is called Beamformer (BFer). The receiver is
          called Beamformee (BFee).
      •   In eTxBF, the quality of sounding handshake process determines the quality of Beamforming data
          streaming.
      •   BFer sends the sounding requests (NDPA packets and NDP) to BFee for channel estimations.
      •   BFee responses the sounding feedback to BFer which containing channel estimations as profile based
          on the NDP transmitter by BFer.
      •   BFer produces a steering matrix from received sounding profiles.
      •   BFer transmits the data packets to BFee by beamformed streams with calibrated energy based on the
          steering matrix.

❑ Downlink Multi-User Multi-Input-Multi-Output (DL MU-MIMO)
   •   Downlink MU-MIMO is a technology based on eTxBF to achieve simultaneous transmission of multiple
       independent data streams for multiple users.
   •   MU-MIMO transmitter as well as BFer utilizes steering matrix to signaling multiple beamformed data
       streams in direction of each MU-MIMO receiver as well as BFee.
   •   After receiving the data packets, each MU-MIMO receiver responses the acknowledgement in a specific

1         Introduction

1.1                    Introduction of Wi-Fi OFDMA

❑ OFDMA
         As efficient use in 4G LTE and 5G, multiple users can be served by different Resource Units(RUs)
          /Bandwidth simultaneously
❑ Uplink Resource Scheduling
         Compared to legacy 802.11, where large users compete each other to send UL data, 11ax provides
          trigger scheduling in better resource utilization and better latency experience
❑ Uplink MUMIMO
         Allow users can send uplink data in the same bandwidth simultaneously for sharing heavy traffic such
          as social media and content sharing
         Assume: 11ax with 4x4 AP and 2x2 Client. It would increase 2x capacity compared to 11ac uplink


      *User also represents Non-AP STA
      *UL: Uplink


1.2                    Introduction of Wi-Fi 7 OFDMA

❑ Why OFDMA in Wi-Fi 7
         RU-OFDMA is mandatory for Wi-Fi 6/7 certification
         Marketing Requirements Document (MRD):
          -         DL/UL OFDMA may increase network throughput for a BSS with many stations
          -         DL/UL OFDMA allows multiple data frames to be transmitted in a single PPDU to multiple stations,
                    thus amortizing preamble overhead and medium contention overhead
❑ What’s new in Wi-Fi 7 OFDMA: Multi-RU (MRU)
         Allow multiple RUs to be assigned to a single user ➔ SU puncturing (non-OFDMA)
         Combine RUs for increased transmission efficiency ➔ MRU support in OFDMA

1      Introduction

       Setting the transmission rate of high-priority packets such as ARP, DHCP, and EAPOL is critical
for ensuring the timely and efficient delivery of these packets, which can improve the overall
performance and reliability of a network.
       High-priority packets are critical for the proper functioning of a network. ARP packets are used
to map network addresses to physical addresses, DHCP packets are used to assign IP addresses and
other network configuration information, and EAPOL packets are used for network authentication and
security. If these packets are not transmitted quickly and efficiently, it can cause delays and disruptions
in the network, leading to performance issues and security vulnerabilities.
       By setting the transmission rate of high-priority packets, network administrators can ensure
that these critical packets are prioritized and transmitted quickly and efficiently, reducing the risk of
delays and disruptions. This, in turn, can improve the overall performance and reliability of the
network, ensuring that critical data is transmitted quickly and accurately.
       Overall, setting the transmission rate of high-priority packets such as ARP, DHCP, and EAPOL is
an important part of network management and can help ensure the efficient and reliable operation of
a network.
       PKT Category
                      ARP / DHCP / PING / EAPOL
       Per Band Setting (not support per bss)
       Rate Range
                      CCK (1/2/5.5/11M)
                      OFDM (6/9/12/18/24/36/48/54M)

       Introduction
In the Wi-Fi field, Single SKU (Single Stock Keeping Unit) refers to a feature that allows manufacturers
to control the transmission power of Wi-Fi devices (such as routers and access points) according to the
radio regulations of different countries and regions. This enables manufacturers to provide products
for different global markets using the same hardware design while ensuring compliance with local
radio regulations.


By dynamically adjusting the transmission power at the firmware or software level, device
manufacturers can reduce product complexity and cost while adhering to regulations, as they don't
need to manufacture different hardware versions for each market. In short, the Single SKU feature
helps device manufacturers more easily meet the requirements of global markets.


In MTK, this power control function consists of the following two sub-parts:
⚫    Single SKU: The maximum TX power value is limited based on different channels, phymodes,
     bandwidth, and phyrates.
⚫    BF Backoff: The maximum TX power value is limited based on different channels, phymodes,
     bandwidth, TX antenna, data stream, and beamform status.

1      Smart Carrier Sense Function description
Smart Carrier Sense (SCS) is a feature that improves the channel access method.


In traditional carrier sense multiple access (CSMA) protocols, such as CSMA/CA used in Wi-Fi, a device
listens for a clear channel before transmitting data. However, if multiple devices are trying to access
the channel at the same time, collisions can occur, resulting in lost packets and lower network
efficiency.
By using SCS, the channel access method becomes more efficient, reducing the likelihood of collisions
and increasing overall network performance. This is especially important in high-density wireless
environments, such as airports, stadiums, and conference centers, where many devices are competing
for the same limited bandwidth.

1      Function description
Spatial Reuse is a technology that maximizes wireless spectrum utilization efficiency by utilizing Spatial
Division Multiple Access (SDMA) technology. Traditional wireless networks typically use time or
frequency division to communicate with multiple users, which is inefficient and prone to interference.
Spatial Reuse, on the other hand, allows multiple devices to communicate on the same time and
frequency by utilizing spatial multiplexing, thereby increasing network throughput and capacity. It is
commonly used in wireless local area networks (WLANs) and wireless metropolitan area networks
(WMANs) and is suitable for high-speed and high-density wireless network scenarios such as airports,
large shopping malls, and conference centers.
In Spatial Reuse technology, the network allocates devices to different spatial areas by utilizing
location information, thereby avoiding interference and conflicts, and further improving network
performance and capacity. In addition, Spatial Reuse technology can be combined with other
technologies such as Beamforming and MU-MIMO to further improve network performance and
capacity. In summary, Spatial Reuse is an efficient wireless network technology that can help improve
network performance and capacity, making wireless networks more suitable for high-density and high-
speed communication scenarios.
In today's environment, dealing with massively crowded scenarios occupied by different Wi-Fi device
signals is a crucial issue. To support simultaneous service, IEEE has included the Spatial Reuse (SR)
technique, which enhances the transmit opportunities of each device in dense environments.

1.1              Introduction

The legacy IEEE specification defines that wireless networks need to follow the Listen before Talk
mechanism to avoid packet collision, also known as CSMA/CA. However, as more and more Wi-Fi
devices are deployed in high-density areas, such as places with high populations, Listen before Talk
restricts each device's transmit opportunity. To solve the issue of inefficient airtime usage in dense
environments, the Spatial Reuse technique is introduced.

1.1.2             What is Spatial Reuse

The IEEE specifies Spatial Reuse (SR) as a mechanism to enhance the Transmit Opportunity via Listen
and Check Before Talk rule. To implement SR, the following steps are taken:
•    Check the BSS color in the PHY header for Wi-Fi 7 or Wi-Fi 6 interference (EHT/HE).
•    Check the MAC address in the MAC header for Legacy interference (EHT/HE/VHT/HT).

3.   Abort Rx and start concurrent transmission."

1          TWT introduction
❑ Target wake time (TWT) allow an AP to manage activity in the BSS by scheduling STAs to operate at
      different times in order to minimize contention and to reduce the required amount of time that a
      STA utilizing a power management mode needs to be awake.
❑ This is achieved by allocating STAs to operate at non-overlapping times and concentrate the frame
      exchanges in predefined service periods.
❑ STAs that request a TWT agreement(AGRT) are called TWT requesting STAs and the STAs which
      respond to their requests are TWT responding STAs.
❑ A TWT requesting STA is assigned specific times to wake and exchange frames with the TWT
      responding STA



1.1                      Types of TWT

❑ Implicit vs Explicit

❑ Announced vs Unannounced
           With/without announcement to receive DL buffered frames


❑ Trigger-enabled vs Non triggered-enabled (11ax)
           The way UL frames are transmitted


❑ Individual vs Broadcast (11ax)
           With/without announcement to receive DL buffered frames

1         Feature Description

1.1                 Beamforming

Beamforming is a signal process technique for directional signal transmission and reception.
There are two kinds of beamforming, one is explicit and the other is implicit.
❑ Implicit Beamforming (iBF)
      •   Implicit beamforming is a Wi-Fi feature that can improve the quality and stability of Wi-Fi signals by
          adjusting the phase and amplitude of the transmitted signals, especially in multi-user environments.
          Implicit beamforming is a passive form of beamforming, as it only involves the transmission of signals,
          rather than the reception of signals. It can automatically adjust the signals to improve Wi-Fi
          performance without the need for advanced algorithms. When user devices support Implicit
          beamforming, they can automatically communicate with the router to coordinate signal adjustments.
          Implicit beamforming is an effective way to improve Wi-Fi coverage and stability, particularly for users
          with older Wi-Fi devices.
❑ Explicit Beamforming (eBF)
      •   Explicit beamforming is an advanced Wi-Fi feature that uses advanced algorithms and techniques to
          adjust the phase and amplitude of Wi-Fi signals, thereby improving Wi-Fi performance. Compared to
          Implicit beamforming, Explicit beamforming is more active and precise, and can adjust signals based on
          the position and environment of the receiver, achieving better results. Explicit beamforming can greatly
          increase the transmission speed and coverage of Wi-Fi, especially in multi-user and multi-antenna
          systems. Explicit beamforming requires routers and user devices that support it, and compatible
          technologies and protocols to implement it. Explicit beamforming is a more advanced Wi-Fi technology
          than Implicit beamforming.

2         eBF ATE Command Format and Execution Flow

2.1                 Command for Golden

❑ mwctl ra0 set ATEConTxETxBfGdProc=TxMode:MCS:BW:Channel:Channel2:ChannelBand
❑ Total 6 parameters
      •   [1] TxMode: (2-digit)
          00 for CCK, 01 for OFDM, 02 for HT-Mixed, 03 for HT-Green, 04 for VHT, 08 for HE, 15 for EHT
      •   [2] MCS: (2-digit)
          MCS rate configuration, we can configure it from 00 to 31 for HT mode, 00 to 09 for VHT mode, 00 to 11
          for HE mode, and 00 to 13 for EHT mode
      •   [3] BW: (2-digit)
          00: 20MHz 01: 40MHz 02: 80MHz 03: 10M 04: 5M 05: 160MHz(160C) 06: 160MHz (160NC)
          12: 320MHz
      •   [4] Channel: (3-digit)
          The central channel number
      •   [5] Channel2: (3-digit format)
          The channel number for the second VHT80 of 160NC. This parameter would be ignored if not testing
          160NC
      •   [6] ChannelBand: (1-digit format)
          0 for G-Band, 1 for 5G-Band, 2 for 6G-Band


2.2                 Command for DUT

❑ mwctl ra0 set
    ATEConTxETxBfInitProc=TxMode:MCS:BW:VhtNss:TRxStream:TxPower:Channel:Channel2:ChannelB
    and:TxPktLength
❑ Total 10 parameters
      •   [1] TxMode: (2-digit)
      •   [2] MCS: (2-digit)
      •   [3] BW: (2-digit)
      •   [4] VhtNss: (2-digit)
          The number of TxStream and the possible value is 01, 02, 03, 04
      •   [5] TRxStream: (2-digit)
          The antenna number for Tx and Rx and the possible value is 01, 02, 03, 04
      •   [6] TxPower: (2-digit)
          The Power DAC value of OFDM 54M target power. Unit is 0.5dBm
      •   [7] Channel: (3-digit)
      •   [8] Channel2: (3-digit format)
      •   [9] ChannelBand: (1-digit format)

1       Introduction
1.1                Overview

This document is a software programming guide for MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 driver on how to configure Wi-Fi settings and how to
run it on OpenWrt. In this guide, we will focus on a few key areas: hostapd/wpa_supplicant, cfg80211, AP full MAC driver,
configuration framework and corresponding features.


cfg80211 is the Linux wireless configuration API that is used for configuring wireless LAN devices. It provides a generic
interface for configuring wireless drivers and devices, allowing them to interact with the Linux kernel and user space.


The AP full MAC driver is responsible for managing the low-level communication between the network hardware and the
operating system. It provides an interface between the hardware and software layers of the network stack, allowing the
operating system to communicate with the wireless hardware. Moreover, it implements the cfg80211 callbacks for
AP/APCLI devices. It then depends on cfg80211 for both registration to the networking subsystem and for configuration, in
which the configuration is utilized by both hostapd/wpa-supplicant services and driver profile initialization.

1.2                  High-Level Architecture


The Wi-Fi driver is mainly composed of two significant modules, mt_wifi and wlan_hwifi. With the proprietary
implementation, it can drive MediaTek’s Wi-Fi 7 based chipsets and offers a rich feature set as specified in IEEE802.11
series standard specifications depending on chipset capabilities.


The design goal of the Wi-Fi driver is to implement a multiple-chipset compatible device driver and allow further control
from the configuration interface supported on different software platforms. To achieve this requirement, the Wi-Fi driver is
implemented as a layering and modularization structure. Figure 1-2 shows the driver architecture, which is a combination
of specific kernel modules, such as mt_wifi and wlan_hwifi.


The laying classification depends on two types – software protocol-related or hardware/hif control-related modules.
mt_wifi is primarily responsible for protocol negotiation, handling packets from Wi-Fi or Ethernet and software related
functions. wlan_hwifi is generally responsible for hardware resource control, packet transmission or reception from Wi-Fi
hardware module and handling device probe/disconnect requests.

To support multiple operating system, mt_wifi_cmn is implemented as OS abstract layer module for mt_wifi to use Linux

changes. The files are in mt_wifi/mk folder. The config files are in mt_wifi/mk/config, while the object files are in

3.1.3              hostapd/wpa_supplicant

With the release of the Wi-Fi 7 AP SDK, hostapd and wpa_supplicant have been officially integrated with the Wi-Fi AP
driver to provide improved coverage for open-source applications. This integration enables better support for open-source
software development and ensures that the Wi-Fi AP driver is compatible with a wider range of applications.


Hostapd is a user space daemon for AP and authentication servers. It implements IEEE 802.11 access point management,
IEEE 802.1X/WPA/WPA2/EAP Authenticators, RADIUS client, EAP server, and RADIUS authentication server. Hostapd is
designed to be a "daemon" program that runs in the background and acts as the backend component controlling
authentication. hostapd supports separate frontend programs and an example text-based frontend, hostapd_cli, is
included with hostapd. For the Wi-Fi driver, hostapd mainly plays the role of bringing up/down AP wireless interfaces that
are registered by driver, configuring SSID, auth mode, encryption type and passphrase, doing 4-way handshake (including
setting key to logan driver) and can support WPS protocol and 802.1X authenticator. The Wi-Fi MLME layer is maintained
within the driver, for instance, the authentication and association frame exchange processes are handled by the state
machine implemented within the driver. Notably, there have been modifications made to the Wi-Fi 7 protocol, which is
maintained by MediaTek through patch files. Consequently, the optimal solution is to use the native hostapd in conjunction
with the MediaTek patches.


Wpa_supplicant is designed to be a "daemon" program for STA that runs in the background and acts as the backend
component controlling the wireless connection. wpa_supplicant supports separate frontend programs and a text-based
frontend (wpa_cli) is included with wpa_supplicant. For the Wi-Fi driver, wpa_supplicant's main function is to bring up the
STA interfaces registered by the Logan driver, receive user commands to configure the target BSS (SSID, authentication
mode, and passphrase, etc.), start scanning, and automatically select the network to connect to. It also performs the 4-way
handshake and sets the key for the Wi-Fi driver. Like hostapd, the optimal solution is to use the native wpa_supplicant in
conjunction with MediaTek patches.


Hostapd and wpa_supplicant communicate with the Wi-Fi driver using NL80211 commands. They utilize the libnl APIs to
send specific NL80211 commands to cfg80211, which in turn invokes hook functions in the Wi-Fi driver. The Wi-Fi driver
also calls cfg80211 APIs when necessary, which triggers cfg80211 to send corresponding NL80211 commands to hostapd
and wpa_supplicant.

3.2                Configuration Framework

UCI provides a unified interface for configuring various system components, including wireless interfaces and system
settings. UCI provides a configuration file for hostapd, which contains the settings for the wireless network interface. This
configuration file is typically located in /etc/config/wireless and contains sections and options that represent different
wireless network settings, such as SSID, encryption method, and authentication method.


The functionality of hostapd can be configured through a configuration file, typically located at /var/run/hostapd/hostapd-
iface.conf. This file contains a set of options that define the behavior of the access point, including the SSID, security
settings, and authentication methods.



3.3                Data Path Processing

3.3.1              TX Data Path

For the TX data path, the rt28xx_send_packets() function serves as the first entry point in the MTK chip Wi-Fi driver. This
function is hooked to the kernel's wireless netDevHook.xmit callback, allowing packets with the SKB structure from the
kernel to be passed into the driver via this function after being hooked.


In the driver, packets are first classified into several types based on QoS. A sanity check is then performed to ensure that
the packets can be transmitted. Afterward, the packets are enqueued into a software queue for priority scheduling, and a
kernel API is called to schedule a tasklet for processing the packets in the software queue. Subsequently, the tasklet
scheduled by the kernel dequeues packets from the software priority queue and parses the packet information into a
tx_blk structure, which is used to carry information between functions in the TX path.

3.3.2              RX Data Path

For the RX path, packets are received from the Wi-Fi chip and moved to the RX ring from HW buffer via WFDMA. This
prompts a HW interrupt to notify the registered Wi-Fi driver that packets have arrived.


The IRQ handler, which is registered by Hwifi driver, then begins processing the RX packets. This handler disables the IRQ
and calls a kernel thread for handling the RX packet.


In the kernel thread of Hwifi driver, an SKB is allocated for the RX Wi-Fi packets, which are dequeued from DMA ring. The
driver then parses the RX descriptor attached by HW into rx_blk, which is used to carry the SKB and additional information.


Next, the rx_blk is passed to AP MAC driver. Based on the payload of the SKB and the information in the RXD, the driver fills
in additional details for packet processing later. The packet is then dispatched to the appropriate handler function
according to its frame type, such as MGMT, CTRL, or Data frame. In the RX data path, the driver searches for station record
table to determine which station the packets belong to and checks if the packets are allowed. Once the station is found,
the driver first performs software block ack (BA) reordering if the packet is QoS data and the station has an established BA
session. After BA reordering, the packets are passed up to the kernel via the netif_rx function, marking the end of the RX
path.


Like the HW TX path, there is a WED RX trap before packets are passed up to the kernel if the HW RX path is supported.
After packets are trapped, the WED module learns the 5-tuple and forwards subsequent packets from the same connection
to the HW RX path.


Furthermore, there is a new HW feature named Rx Reorder Offload (RRO) module that supports packet reordering by HW.
If supported, the chip performs packet reordering before moving the packets to the host. Conversely, the host driver does
not need to perform packet reordering if it has already been done in the RRO module.

3.4                Multi-Link Operation

Multi-Link Operation (MLO) enables the simultaneous operation over multiple links, managed by an MLD. Communication
across different frequency bands or channels can occur simultaneously or not, depending on the capabilities of both the AP
MLD and the non-AP MLD.


The MLO procedures allow a pair of MLDs to discover, synchronize, (de)authenticate, (re)associate, disassociate, and manage
resources with each other on any common bands or channels supported by both MLDs




                                          Figure 3-8. Example MLD and affiliated STA communication system

Access point (AP) multi-link device (MLD): An MLD, where each station (STA) affiliated with the MLD is an AP.


Affiliated STA: A station (STA), which can be an access point (AP) STA or non-access point (non-AP) STA, which provides link-
specific, lower medium access protocol (MAC) services within a multi-link device (an MLD).


Extremely high throughput (EHT) basic service set (BSS): A BSS in which the transmitted Beacon frame includes an EHT
Operation element.

Multi-link device (MLD): A logical entity that can support more than one affiliated station (STA) but can also operate using

Multi-link operation (MLO): Operations between two multi-link devices (MLDs) as described in 35.3 (Multi-link operation).


Multi-Link probe request: A Probe Request frame that is transmitted by a station (STA) affiliated with a non-access point
(non-AP) multi-link device (MLD) carrying Probe Request Multi-Link element to solicit information of one or more APs
affiliated with an AP MLD.

device (MLD) carrying Basic Multi-Link element in response to a Multi-Link probe request to provide complete profile or
requested information of one or more APs affiliated with an AP MLD.


Multi-radio non-access point (non-AP) multi-link device (MLD): A non-AP MLD that supports reception or transmission of
frames on more than one link at a time.


Non-simultaneous transmit and receive (NSTR) link pair: A pair of links within a multi-link device (an MLD) for which the
receiver requirements specified in Clause 36 (Extremely high throughput (EHT) PHY specification) are not met on one of the
links when a station (STA) of the MLD is transmitting on the other link. Each link of such a pair is a member of the NSTR link
pair.


Non-access point (non-AP) multi-link device (MLD): An MLD, where each station (STA) affiliated with the MLD is a non-AP
STA.


Simultaneous transmit and receive (STR) link pair: A pair of links that is not a non-simultaneous transmit and receive (NSTR)
link pair.


Single radio non-access point (non-AP) multi-link device (MLD): A non-AP MLD that supports operation on more than one
link but receives or transmits frames only on one link at a time.

3.4.2              MLO Operation Mode

One of the key features of IEEE 802.11be is operation mode support of Multi-Link Devices (MLDs). In this context, it is
essential to understand the different types of MLO supporting modes, such as STR and EMLSR.


Simultaneous transmit and receive (STR)


The signal isolation between different links is sufficient so that the links can operate independently and are capable of
transmitting and receiving simultaneously in different links. STR is different from legacy single link (SL) STA and legacy dual
band dual concurrent (DBDC) STA, STAs affiliated with a STA MLD share a common transmitter sequence number (SN) and a
common space for data transmission allocated to different links if multiple link’s transmission has the same access category
(AC). This property allows MLD to more quickly transmit an application’s data packets among different links and naturally
reduces latency performance.

4        Cfg80211 Control Interface
4.1                Introduction

cfg80211 and nl80211 are two important components in the Linux wireless networking stack that provide the interface
between the kernel and user-space applications.


cfg80211 is a Linux kernel subsystem that provides the core wireless networking functions for both station and access point
modes. It defines a set of APIs that enable wireless devices and drivers to communicate with the kernel and with user-
space applications.


The main functionality of cfg80211 includes:
• Managing wireless network interfaces
• Scanning for available wireless networks
• Connecting to wireless networks
• Authenticating and associating with wireless access points
• Managing wireless regulatory domain settings
• Handling wireless events, such as link status changes, roaming, and authentication failures.


nl80211 is the user-space interface for cfg80211, providing a standardized set of commands and events for configuring and
monitoring wireless devices. It is implemented as a netlink socket protocol and enables user-space applications to interact
with the cfg80211 subsystem.


The main functionality of nl80211 includes:
• Configuring and managing wireless interfaces, such as enabling and disabling wireless devices and setting interface
    parameters.
• Scanning for available wireless networks
• Configuring wireless network parameters, such as SSID, channel, and security settings
• Monitoring wireless events, such as link status changes, received signal strength, and channel utilization.


nl80211 is used by various user-space applications such as the wpa_supplicant daemon, which provides support for Wi-Fi
authentication and encryption, and the hostapd daemon, which provides support for Wi-Fi access point functionality.

5       Configuration Mode
5.1                Universal Control Interface (UCI)

One important aspect of OpenWrt is its use of the Universal Control Interface (UCI), which provides a simple and flexible
way to manage the configuration of the system.


In terms of architecture, UCI is built on top of the OpenWrt system architecture and provides a unified interface for
managing configuration data. It consists of a set of command-line tools and configuration files that allow users to view,
edit, and apply configuration settings. The UCI system is organized around a hierarchical data structure, with each
configuration setting represented as a node in the tree. This structure makes it easy to navigate and manage the
configuration data.


Functionally, UCI provides a flexible way to manage the configuration of OpenWrt devices. It allows users to configure a
wide range of settings, including network interfaces, firewall rules, wireless networks, system settings, and more. UCI is
designed to be easy to use and easy to understand, even for users who are not familiar with the underlying system
architecture. For example, users can use simple command-line tools like "uci show" to view the current configuration, or
"uci set" to modify a specific setting.



5.2                /etc/config/wireless

The wireless radio UCI configuration is located in /etc/config/wireless.
• wifi-device: specifies general radio properties such as channel, driver type and txpower.
• wifi-iface: defines a wireless network on the top of a Wi-Fi device
• wifi-mld: define a wireless MLD group on the top of Wi-Fi interfaces.

           /lib/wif/mtkdat.lua                                               /lib/wifi/mtwifi.lua                                                   /lib/wifi/supplicant.lua




         /lib/wifi/quick_setting.lua                                        /lib/wifi/ wifi_services.lua                                               /lib/wifi/hostapd.lua




- `mtwifi.lua` - This library is an interface between `/sbin/wifi` and the MTK Wi-Fi driver. It calls functions from `mtkdat.lua`,
`hostapd.lua`, and `supplicant.lua` to provide functionality for "wifi save", "wifi detect", "wifi up", "wifi down", "wifi
restart", and "wifi reload".


- `mtkdat.lua` - This library is responsible for converting UCI configurations to profile configurations or generating initial UCI
configurations based on profile configurations. Additionally, it provides a set of Lua APIs for use in other Lua scripts.


- `hostapd.lua` - This library translates UCI configurations to hostapd configurations and provides the functionality to bring
up or down AP interfaces.


- `supplicant.lua` - This library translates UCI configurations to wpa_supplicant configurations and provides the
functionality to bring up or down STA interfaces.


- `quicksetting.lua` - This library provides a fast way to reload Wi-Fi configurations without needing to bring down and up
the Wi-Fi interface. It achieves this by comparing the old and new profile configuration and executing relevant `mwctl`,
`hostapd_cli`, or `wpa_cli` commands based on the differences.


- `wifi_services.lua` - This library manages the Wi-Fi service based on the state of the Wi-Fi driver.


Together, these Lua scripts provide a comprehensive set of functionality for configuring and managing MTK Wi-Fi 7 driver.
By converting the wireless UCI configuration file into band profiles and WPAd configuration files, these scripts enable easy
and flexible configuration of Wi-Fi interfaces, while the other scripts provide additional functionality for Wi-Fi
management.

7        mWDS
mWDS, or Mesh Wireless Distribution System, is a feature of Wi-Fi that allows for the creation of a wireless mesh network.
In this network, nodes can communicate with each other directly, as well as through intermediary nodes, without the need
for a wired infrastructure.


The main functionality of mWDS is to provide a wireless mesh network that can be used to extend the coverage and
capacity of a Wi-Fi network. This can be especially useful in situations where a wired infrastructure is not feasible or
desirable, such as in outdoor or remote locations.


MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 drivers support AP-to-STA WDS mode to use wireless bridging to form one common broadcast domain
based on executing a normal association procedure (authentication request/response, association request/response).


In MWDS (Mixed WDS) mode, the management/control frames are transmitted in 3-address and the data frame types are
transmitted in 4-address.

8       WPS
The Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS) is also known as Wi-Fi Simple Configuration. It is a standard feature that simplifies the
process of setting up protected connections for various Wi-Fi devices connecting to APs. Although WPS is not yet popular,
it is a very useful configuration method that helps users avoid manually configuring SSID and security to create a WLAN.



8.1                WPS Scenarios

There are two kinds of WPS scenarios. One is to set up a new WLAN and the other is to add new member devices to an
existing WLAN. Initial WLAN setup is what a user must do after buying a new AP device. After initial WLAN setup is
complete, AP is ready to accept connection requests from client devices. Then, it is necessary to adding Member Devices.
The following list describes all the possible scenarios when using WPS. The terminology used here would be introduced in
the next section


Initial WLAN Setup
• Standalone AP with a built-in Registrar
    – WPS is not needed in this case
• AP and an External Registrar
    – EAP-based setup of External Wireless Registrar
       ▪ [AP as Enrollee] --- EAP --- [Wireless Registrar]
    – UPnP-based setup of External Wired Registrar
       ▪ [AP as Enrollee] --- UPnP --- [Wired Registrar]
• Adding Member Devices
    – In-band setup using a standalone AP/Registrar
       ▪ [STA Enrollee] --- EAP --- [AP/Registrar]
    – In-band setup using an External Registrar
    – UPnP-based setup of External Wireless Registrar
       ▪ [STA Enrollee] --- EAP --- [AP] --- UPnP --- [Wireless Registrar]
    – UPnP-based setup of External Wired Registrar
       ▪ [STA Enrollee] --- EAP --- [AP] --- UPnP --- [Wired Registrar]


*EAP stands for Extensible Authentication Protocol
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extensible_Authentication_Protocol
*UPnP stands for Universal Plug and Play
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universal_Plug_and_Play



8.2                Architectural Overview

This section presents high-level description of the Wi-Fi Simple Configuration architecture. Most material is taken directly
from the WSC specification. In the following figure, you can see that there are three logical components involved in WSC:
the Registrar, the access point (AP), and the Enrollee

[Component]
The Enrollee is a device seeking to join a WLAN domain. Once an Enrollee obtains a valid credential, it becomes a member.
The Registrar is an entity with the authority to issue and revoke domain credentials. A registrar may be integrated into an
AP, or it may be separate from the AP.
The AP is an infrastructure mode 802.11 Access Point. We also call it Proxy.


[Interface]
Interface E is logically located between the Enrollee and the Registrar and its purpose is to enable the Registrar to discover
and issue WLAN credentials to the Enrollee.


Interface M is between the AP and the Registrar and it enables an external Registrar to manage a WSC AP.


Interface A is between the Enrollee and the AP and it enables discovery of the WSC WLAN and communication between
the Enrollee and IP-only Registrars.

8.9.3              WPS Configuration Status

The WPS attribute “Simple Configuration (SC) State” in WPS IEs (contained in beacon and probe response) indicates
whether an AP DUT is configured.




If an AP is shipped from the factory in an un-configured state (SC State is 0x01), then the AP must change to the configured
state (SC State is 0x02) if any of the following occurs.
• Automatic configuration via WPS by an external Registrar
   The AP sends the WSC_Done message in the External Registrar configuration process.
• Automatic configuration via WPS by an internal Registrar
   The AP receives the WSC_Done response in the Enrollee Registration Process from the first Enrollee. The internal
   registrar waits until successful completion of the protocol before applying the automatically generated credentials to
   avoid an accidental transition from un-configured to configured one in the case that a neighbouring device tries to run

   WSC before the real enrollee, but fails. A failed attempt does not change the configuration of the AP, nor the Simple
   Config State.
• Manual configuration by user
   One user manually configures the AP using whatever interface(s) it provides to modify any one of the followings:
   – SSID
   – Encryption method
   – Authentication method
   – Any key or pass phrase


If an AP is shipped from the factory in an un-configured state (SC State 0x01), then a Factory Reset must revert the Simple
Config State to be un-configured. If an AP is shipped from the factory pre-configured with WPA2PSK and a randomly
generated key, the SC State must be 'Configured' (0x02) so as to prevent an external Registrar from overwriting the default
factory settings. A factory reset must restore the DUT to the same configuration as what it was when shipped.

9         Channel, Scan and ACS
MediaTek Wi-Fi 7 driver supports three radio frequency bands in Wi-Fi communications: 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz. The
channel list supported on each band depends on the region configuration.


Channel switch may be triggered by the end user, radar hit on DFS channel, DFS-ZW state machine, scan, or ACS.
Those channel related features (channel switch, scan, ACS, DFS) are all implemented in the MTK driver.


9.1                 Channel

6G PSC
      •   With 1200 MHz of spectrum and 59 new 20 MHz channels, a station with a dwell time of 200ms per channel
          would require almost 12 seconds to complete a passive scan of the entire band. The 802.11ax spec defines an
          efficient process for clients to discover nearby access points (APs).
      •   In Wi-Fi 6E, a process called fast passive scanning is being used to focus on a reduced set of channels called
          preferred scanning channels (PSC). PSCs are a set of 15 20-MHz channels that are spaced every 80MHz. The APs
          will set their primary channel to coincide with the PSC so that it can be easily discovered by a client, and clients
          will use passive scanning to scan only on PSCs to look for an AP.


Channel related configuration depends on /etc/config/wireless and MTK proprietary profile.
In Cert Mode (WifiCert=1 in MTK proprietary profile), channel/BW settings in hostapd config file will also be applied to Wi-

An AP shall inform associated STAs that the AP is moving to a new channel and maintain the association by advertising the
switch using Channel Switch Announcement (CSA) elements in Beacon frames and Probe Response frames until the
intended channel switch time. Through the CSA elements and the channel switch procedure, the connection can be kept
during channel updating on peers.

If an AP affiliated with an AP MLD is switching channel, the Channel Switch Announcement element, the Extended
Channel Switch Announcement element, and the Max Channel Switch Time element will be included in every Beacon and
Probe Response frames on all links of the AP MLD from right after the time the AP includes the elements in the Beacon
frame it transmits until the intended channel switch time.


Another AP (reporting AP) affiliated with the same AP MLD shall carry the corresponding element(s) in the STA Profile field
of the Per-STA Profile sub-element corresponding to the affected AP contained in the Basic Multi-Link element included in
the Beacon frame and Probe Response frame that it transmits.


On an MLD connection, the channel switch notification has the chance to be carried on multi-links, which will make the
channel synchronize mechanism more reliable. The behavior is described as below:
If the CSA is disabled, AP will send De-Auth out and then the clients need to reconnect.


When the CSA is enabled, AP will append CSA IE on all MLO link to keep connection during channel switching.
• AP
   – Append CSA IEs in COM_IE of beacon/probe_response on channel switching link;
   – Append Max_channel_switch_time IE in COM_IE of beacon/probe_response;
   – Append CSA IEs in mlo per_sta_profile of beacon/probe_response on other mlo links;
   – Append Max_channel_switch_time IE in per_sta_profile of MLO of beacon/probe_response on other mlo links;
   – Trigger critical update on all links;
   – Update RNR according to PHY channel setting.
• APCli
   – Parse CSA IEs in COM_IE/MLD_IE of beacon/probe_response, do channel switch on corresponding link

9.3                 Scan

Scan is used to collect outside AP information and the channel utilization information.


Two scan methods are available: active and passive.
Active scan is done through sending multiple probe requests and recording the probe responses. Passive scanning, on the

9.4                 ACS

ACS scan stands for Automatic Channel Selection. It is a feature in Wi-Fi that allows the AP to automatically scan and select
the best available channel to operate on.


The ACS scan feature provides several benefits to Wi-Fi networks, including:
1.    Improved Performance: By automatically selecting the best channel, the access point can avoid interference from
      other Wi-Fi networks, Bluetooth devices, and other sources of RF noise. This can result in improved throughput and
      reduced latency.
2.    Simplified Deployment: With ACS scan enabled, administrators do not need to manually configure the Wi-Fi channel
      for each access point. This can simplify the deployment process and reduce the likelihood of configuration errors.


Dynamic Channel Selection: As the Wi-Fi spectrum changes over time, the ACS scan feature can automatically adjust the
channel selection to ensure optimal performance. This can improve the overall reliability and availability of the Wi-Fi
network.

10 WMM
Wireless Multimedia (WMM) is a Quality of Service (QoS) protocol that is included in the Wi-Fi architecture. It is designed
to improve the quality of multimedia applications such as voice and video over a Wi-Fi network.


WMM consists of four Access Categories (AC): AC_VO (Voice), AC_VI (Video), AC_BE (Best Effort), and AC_BK (Background).
These access categories prioritize traffic based on the type of application and the required QoS. The Voice and Video
access categories prioritize traffic that requires low latency and jitter, such as voice and video applications. Best Effort
prioritizes traffic that requires a moderate level of QoS, such as email and web browsing. Background prioritizes traffic that
requires a low level of QoS, such as file downloads and software updates. This allows Wi-Fi networks to provide a better
user experience for voice and video applications while ensuring fair access to the wireless medium for all devices.

10.3               DSCP-WMM Priority Mapping

For interworking with IP networks, a map is devised between the 802.11e user priorities and the IP differentiated services
code point (DSCP).


Mapping is specified as DSCP ranges to individual user priority values, and as a set of exceptions with one-to-one mapping

11 IEEE802.11h
IEEE 802.11h is a 2003 amendment added to the IEEE 802.11 standard for Spectrum and Transmit Power Management
Extensions. It addresses problems like interference with satellites and radar using the same 5 GHz frequency band. It was

Dynamic Frequency Selection (DFS) and Transmit Power Control (TPC) to the 802.11a PHY. It has since been integrated into
the full IEEE 802.11-2007 standard.

12 AP-CLIENT
The AP-Client function provides a simulated and virtual STA interface while the original AP interface is working
simultaneously. Its application is usually a wireless repeater or a wireless extender. AP-Client mainly provides a 1-to-N MAC
address mapping mechanism such that multiple stations connected to the AP can transparently communicate with another
AP, which we usually call RootAP. When AP-Client function is enabled, besides the original AP interface named ra0, a virtual
interface named apcli0 will be created. In a repeater application, the software bridge, like br0, is used to relay packets
between these two interfaces. The following figure shows the common network topology and operation module of our AP-
Client function.




AP1 is an Access Point that enabled AP-Client and therefore has two wireless interfaces, ra0 and apcli0, providing the AP
and station function respectively. AP2 is just a traditional Access Point that provides normal AP function. In the figure, you
can see that STA1 is associated with AP1 and STA4 associated with AP2. In the old days, if STA1 wants to communicate with
STA4, AP1 and AP2 must have some kind of connection between them to relay traffic, like Ethernet LAN (wired) or WDS
(wireless). Now with the new AP-Client feature, AP1 can use the simulated STA interface apcli0 to connect to AP2, thus
creating the link, and then STA1 can communicate with STA4 transparently and wired stations connected to AP1 through
Ethernet could also communicate with STA4


Here are some reminders for you before using AP-Client.


AP-Client only supports the following protocols due to the limitation of 1-to-N MAC address mapping mechanism
• All IP-based network applications
• ARP
• DHCP
• PPPoE

13 IGMP Snooping
IGMP Snooping provides a mechanism converting multicast traffic into unicast traffic.


When AP receives incoming multicast traffic, the conversion would be done based on a Multicast Filter Table.
In most scenarios, where media is being streamed, unicast is preferred over multicast. Multicast traffic is subject to packet
loss that can cripple media quality, and unicast traffic can operate at higher data rates.



13.1                 Multicast Packet Parsing Process

Under the cut-through architecture, IGMP m2u guides the MDP module to complete the header translation from 802.3 to
802.11 by using the DAS field and wcid field in the TXD, and filling Addr1, which is RA, with the MAC address of the
corresponding STA.


The important func is igmp_snoop_non_offload(), which completes the process of checking the multicast filter tables and
do pkt clone.


The main code flow is like below:
rt28xx_send_packets()
     -> rt28xx_packet_xmit()
       -> fp_send_data_pkt()
         -> if multicast pkt, igmp_snoop_non_offload()
            -> IgmpPktInfoQuery()
            -> IgmpPktClone()
         -> qm_ops->enq_dataq_pkt
         -> tm_qm_ops->schedule_task
And then dequeue and tx.

15 Fixed Rate
15.1                 Introduction

The fixed rate command is a valuable tool used for Wi-Fi data rate debugging. It provides with the ability to address and
troubleshoot issues related to data transmission in wireless communication.


In a typical scenario, users may encounter poor Wi-Fi performance on their devices and suspect that the data rate at which
the device is communicating with the Wi-Fi network is the root cause. For example, data rate can be set to a fixed value of
MCS-11 using the fixed rate command. This allows the “support team” to observe and analyze the impact of the fixed data
rate on Wi-Fi performance. By doing so, they can identify potential issues such as interference, signal strength, or
compatibility problems that may be affecting the data transmission.


By providing detailed instructions on how to use the fixed rate command, one can fine-tune the data rate settings based on
the observed results and make informed decisions regarding optimizations or configuration changes.

15.3               Data Rate Table

15.3.1             802.11n

The data rate in 802.11n networks is determined by various factors, including the modulation scheme, guard interval, and
frame aggregation. The modulation scheme refers to the method used to encode data onto the wireless signal, while the
guard interval is the timing between symbols. Frame aggregation allows multiple data frames to be combined into a single
transmission, reducing overhead and increasing efficiency.


To understand the relationships between these variables and the resulting data rate, a data rate table is often used. This
table provides a comprehensive overview of the different combinations of modulation schemes, guard intervals, and frame
aggregation settings, along with their corresponding data rates.

15.3.2             802.11ac

The 802.11ac standard introduces several enhancements to achieve higher data rates and better network efficiency. These
enhancements include wider channel bandwidths, more efficient modulation schemes, and the use of multiple-input
multiple-output (MIMO) technology. By utilizing these advancements, 802.11ac can deliver faster and more reliable
wireless connections.


To understand the data rates supported by 802.11ac networks, a data rate table is often used. This table provides a
comprehensive overview of the different combinations of modulation coding schemes (MCS), spatial streams, and channel
bandwidths, along with their corresponding data rates. The MCS values represent the modulation and coding sets used to
encode data onto the wireless signal.

15.3.3            802.11ax

The 802.11ax standard, also known as Wi-Fi 6, aims to address the challenges of dense user environments and the
increasing demand for high-bandwidth applications. One of the key aspects of 802.11ax is its ability to support many
devices simultaneously while maintaining high data rates.


The 802.11ax data rate table introduces a significant increase in the number of available data rates compared to previous
standards. With the introduction of new MCS values and the support for up to 8 spatial streams, 802.11ax offers a wide
range of options for optimizing data rates based on specific network requirements and device capabilities.


For more detailed information on the 802.11ax standard and the data rate table, you can refer to the following resources:
Wi-Fi 6 Wikipedia Page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wi-Fi_6) or https://semfionetworks.com/blog/mcs-table-updated-

15.3.4             802.11be

The 802.11be standard, also known as Wi-Fi 7, is the new generation of wireless networking technology that aims to
provide even higher data rates, lower latency, and improved overall performance compared to previous standards. This
amendment introduces standardized modifications to both the IEEE Std 802.11 physical layers (PHY) and the Medium
Access Control Layer (MAC). These modifications enable at least one mode of operation capable of supporting a maximum
throughput of at least 30 Gbit/s, as measured at the MAC data service access point (SAP), with carrier frequency operation
between 1 and 7.250 GHz. This ensures backward compatibility and coexistence with legacy IEEE Std 802.11 compliant
devices operating in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands.


The 802.11be Data Rate Table, as part of this amendment, provides detailed information about the data rates supported by
the new EHT PHY specification. It includes various modulation classes and their corresponding data rates, providing a
comprehensive overview of the data transmission capabilities of the new standard.


For more detailed information on the 802.11be standard and its features, you can refer to the following resources:
IEEE 802.11be Wikipedia Page (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IEEE_802.11be)

19 Power Percentage
The purpose of this power percentage function is to reduce the target TX power by a percentage. The default TX power
percentage is 100%. You can utilize MTK proprietary profile to control the TX power percentage when the system boots up,
and use the mwctl commands to control it at runtime.



19.1               Enable or Disable Power Percentage

• To enable/disable power percentage, the following setting should be added in MTK proprietary profile:
    – MTK proprietary profile of 2G
       vi /etc/wireless/mediatek/mt7990.b0.dat
       …
              PERCENTAGEenable=x
    – MTK proprietary profile of 5G
       vi /etc/wireless/mediatek/mt7990.b1.dat
       …
              PERCENTAGEenable=x
    – MTK proprietary profile of 6G
       vi /etc/wireless/mediatek/mt7990.b2.dat
       …
              PERCENTAGEenable=x


•     You can also use the following command to enable/disable power percentage at runtime:
       mwctl dev <devname> set pwr PercentageCtrl=x


       x=0: Disable.
       x=1: Enable.



19.2               Set Power Drop Percentage

• To set power drop percentage, the following setting should be added in MTK proprietary profile:
    – MTK proprietary profile of 2G
       vi /etc/wireless/mediatek/mt7990.b0.dat
       …
              TxPower=x
    – MTK proprietary profile of 5G
       vi /etc/wireless/mediatek/mt7990.b1.dat
       …
              TxPower=x

20.6               Kernel Panic Debug Tips

20.6.1             Kernel Panic Log

Kernel panic refers to the actions taken by the operating system when it detects an internal fatal error and cannot safely
handle the error.


A kernel panic log looks like the following picture:




Actual log content depends on your kernel version and configurations, but the concept is similar.
“pc” shows the address of the instruction that caused a panic.
“lr” contains the return address from the last function called prior to a panic.


So, this log means “BssTableDeleteEntry+0xe4” calls “__memcpy”, and then a fatal error occurs at “__memcpy+0x100” that
causes a kernel panic.

20.6.2             How to Locate the Crash Point

In the previous section, you can locate the function that causes a kernel panic. But if you would like to locate the exact line
in the function further, you need to prepare the following items for analysis:


When Wi-Fi driver is built-in:
1.   vmlinux.o at
e.g. openwrt/build_dir/target-xxx/linux-mediatek_yyy/linux-zzz
Actual path depends on your project, SDK version, kernel version, etc.
2.   The .c and .o file that includes the function that causes panic (__memcpy() in our example).
3.   The .c and .o file that includes the function that calls the function in item 2 (BssTableDeleteEntry() in this example).
4.   The complete kernel panic log.


When Wi-Fi driver is ko module:
1.   mt_wifi.ko at
e.g. openwrt/build_dir/target-xxx/linux-mediatek_yyy/mt_wifi/mt_wifi_ap
Actual path depends on your project, SDK version, kernel version, etc.
2.   The .c and .o file that includes the function that causes panic (__memcpy() in our example).
3.   The .c and .o file that includes the function that calls the function in item 2 (BssTableDeleteEntry() in this example).
4.   The complete kernel panic log.


The files should be the same as the version of the issue.


For example, if Wi-Fi driver is ko module, you can utilize some tools to locate the exact line in object files like gdb, objdump
and addr2line at
e.g. openwrt/staging_dir/toolchain-xxx/bin
Actual path and tools depend on your project, SDK version, etc.



20.6.3             Debug Tips Summary

1.   When a kernel panic occurs, follow the instructions above to perform an analysis first
2.   If you cannot find the cause, please provide the necessary files listed in the previous instructions
3.   Please describe the reproduction steps, testing topology, reproduction rate, etc.
4.   Please provide the chipset information, SDK version, driver/firmware version. See 20.2.
5.   Please try to use MediaTek reference image or original driver to clarify the problem.

1       MAP Introduction

1.1           Introduction

MAP (Multi-AP) is a WFA specification whose purpose is to enable inter-operability across Wi-Fi access points
(APs) from different vendors in a Wi-Fi network deployment comprising of multiple APs. It defines the control
protocols between Wi-Fi access points (APs) as well as the data objects necessary to enable onboarding,
provisioning, control and management of APs in a Multiple-AP Wi-Fi network. This specification also defines the
mechanism to route traffic between Wi-Fi access points within the Multi-AP network.

A Multi-AP network consists of two types of logical entities:
         • One Multi-AP Controller and
         • One or more Multi-AP Agents

A Multi-AP Controller is a logical entity in a Multi-AP network that implements logic for controlling the fronthaul
APs and backhaul links in the Multi-AP network

A Multi-AP Agent is a logical entity that executes the Multi-AP Controller functions, and reports measurements
and capabilities data for fronthaul APs, clients and backhaul links to a Multi-AP Controller and/or to other Multi-
AP Agents

Mediatek MAP turnkey solution provides implementation of MAP specification features as well as proprietary
features which help in smooth functioning of Multi-AP networks.

Wi-Fi Alliance has published multiple revisions for the MAP specification. Each revision is named as R1, R2, R3
and so on. Compared with R1, R2 has further improved and standardized Wi-Fi functions, such as Wi-Fi
diagnostics, channel selection and traffic separation. Similarly, with R3 some new features were added like DPP
onboarding for providing more flexibility and security. Then MediaTek Turnkey solution has also kept enhancing
along with each MAP revision to provide enhanced functionality of existing features and spec compliance
directed by new revisions. Below is the WFA timeline history for MAP revisions:

1.4            MLO MAP device
802.11be introduces a concept of a Multi-Link Device (MLD), they support Multi Link Operation (MLO). Legacy
devices which support Single Link Operation (SLO) is referred as Single-Link Devices (SLD) in specificiation. Some
key points about a MLD are as follows:


      •    MLD consists of several so-called affiliated Wi-Fi devices (each has a PHY interface to the wireless media),
           but with a single interface to the LLC layer. The upper-layer protocols consider the MLD as a single device.
      •    Despite having multiple physical radio interfaces, MLD has a single MAC address, and the sequence
           numbers are generated uniquely from the same sequence number space. They allow packet
           retransmission on any link regardless of the link of the initial transmission of the packet.
      •    Each link of an MLD is regarded as a conventional single-link station (STA), and an MLD is a device
           affiliated with more than one STA. In contrast, an SLD (legacy device) is affiliated with only a single STA.
      •    MLDs can be further classified into two types based on the type of the affiliated STAs:
                 • AP multi-link device (AP MLD): each of the affiliated STAs is an AP.
                 • Non-AP multi-link device (non-AP MLD): each of the affiliated STAs is a non-AP (client) STA.

2.2           Driver
Driver exposes interfaces for WAPP to get/set parameters, send/receive data. It uses ioctl and netlink to interact
with WAPP. Driver also provides the capability of 802.11V BTM, 802.11 fast roaming, 802.11 neighbor report,
WPS procedure, WDS 4 address format, MBO.

2.3           WAPP
WAPP (Wi-Fi App) encapsulates different ioctl and netlink event which are access to Wi-Fi driver part, so it may
supply services for other application. Application accessing Wi-Fi resources through WAPP does not need to
know the difference of Wi-Fi drivers, this makes it easier for upper layer applications to port from one generation
of Wi-Fi chipset to another.
WAPP collects common Wi-Fi information of all Wi-Fi interfaces on the same device. Information such as BSS
capability, RSSI, TX power, operating channel, number of clients, are managed in WAPP. For Wi-Fi functions that
requires to get information from driver before making decision, they can take the common information stored
in WAPP instead of send queries to drivers. WAPP also handles IAPP Daemon which is mandatory for 802.11R.

2.3.1         Wappctrl
WAPP control interface is used to control WAPP by using commands of another application called “wappctrl”.
These commands, which are implemented in WAPP with a pre-defined format, can be used to do manual test,
feature development, or debug.

2.3.2         Libwpactrl

2.4           1905 daemon
1905 daemon is used to receive, send and process protocol related messages. It has two kinds of role, controller
and agent. That is to say different role has different logic in message processing. User needs explicitly assign a
role to the daemon when starting up it. Every 1905 device needs to maintain topology database. The 1905
daemon will announce its interface list and attribute by topology response to help other device learn the
fronthaul bss of the device. And step by step, every device in the same topology knows the information of
adjacent and non-adjacent device. There is no need for user to care about wireless interface. The information of
wireless interface will be created by WAPP. User only need explicitly assign Ethernet interface in 1905d.cfg. In
this file, there are two more parameters that need to be configured by the user.
• Every 1905 device needs to assign one unique abstract mac which is called ALMAC. 1905 daemon needs to
receive packets from driver.
• All net devices are bridged to bridge interface. 1905 needs to get the bridge interface to create raw socket to
monitor packets.
For more details and layout of 1905d.cfg file, please refer to Appendix section 10.18.

2.4.1         1905_ctrl
1905 ctrl daemon is used to send cmd to 1905 daemon. This daemon will only be used for passing WFA MAP
certification. In MAP certification, UCC will send bss configuration information and 1905 raw data to 1905
daemon. This information will be written to a file in specific format. 1905 ctrl daemon will send cmd with file
path to 1905 daemon. Then 1905 daemon will parse the event and do related works.



2.5           Mapfilter
Mapfilter is a kernel module that needs to be inserted into kernel before 1905 daemon is started. 1905 daemon
needs to get the net device mac of received packets. It will use this information to maintain neighbor list and
send message back to peer. Mapfilter will maintain a table based on source address of the packets and the net
device mac address which received the packets. 1905 daemon will get net device mac based on source mac by
sockopt.

2.6           MAP Daemon
MAP daemon is an application which implements turnkey features of Mediatek Turnkey MAP solution. It interacts
with both WAPP and 1905 daemon to implement both driver specific and MAP specification specific features
respectively.

2.6.1         MAPD_ctrl
MAPD ctrl daemon is used to send commands to MAP daemon. This daemon is used for testing/configuring
various turnkey features by means of mapd_cli commands. A cumulative list of all mapd_cli commands can be
in the Appendix section 10.13.

3        MAP Network formation and support

3.1           Introduction
MAP network formation refers to the process of agents getting onboarded to the MAP network via a controller
or existing agents. An onboarded Multi-AP Agent gains layer-2 connectivity onto a Multi-AP network through Wi-
Fi or wired connectivity. Till MAP R1/R2 only one onboarding technique was used i.e. WPS Onboarding. With
Map R3 specification a new onboarding technique has also been added i.e. DPP based onboarding. This chapter
describes all aspects of the various onboarding techniques as provided by MediaTek’s turnkey solution. Later
sections of this chapter describe the other support feature which help in network formation.

3.2           MAP Onboarding and Auto-Configuration

Onboarding is the process by which a Multi-AP Agent gains layer-2 connectivity onto a Multi-AP network through
Wi-Fi or wired connectivity. The specification defines methods for onboarding by which a Multi-AP device can
onboard to a Multi-AP network and they have been made part of the MediaTek turnkey solution. Till MAP R1/R2
only one onboarding technique was used i.e. WPS Onboarding. With Map R3 specification a new onboarding
technique has also been added i.e. DPP based onboarding. Each of these techniques have been introduced in
below sections.

Once layer-2 connectivity is established, the multi-AP agent commences the discovery of Multi-AP controller.
The specification enables Multi-AP controller to configure 802.11 interfaces (BSS) on each radio(s) of a Multi-AP
agent. For this process, Agent will use the AP-Autoconfiguration process defined in the 1905 specification.

3.2.1         Configuration Settings
Onboarding and Autoconfiguration require some configuration settings to be done at the controller. When the
controller performs auto configuration of an enrollee agent, then it consults the wts_bss_info_config file which
stores the configuration that controller will apply to new agents.
User needs to set this configuration in the file. There are 2 ways of setting the configuration:
1. Agent specific configuration:
              • User can set the configuration for a particular Agent by specifying the AL MAC address of the
                  agent in the configuration
              • User need make sure the backhaul bss setting on agent need be the same with the whole MAP
                  network. The fronthaul bss setting can be different with the other MAP network. Agent need
                  use its backhaul bss setting to reconnect to MAP network in wifi case.
2. Generic configuration:
              • For rest of the agents, generic configuration is used which is specified by mentioning wildcard
                  AL MAC in the configuration ( FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF)

For sample data of the “wts_bss_info_config” file , please refer to the Appendix section 10.10.
If there is a space in SSID, the user needs to enter \ as ESC in front of it in wts file. This is because space is regarded
as a separator in wts file. If ssid has \, then user needs to add \ as ESC in front of it.
For WPS to be successful, there must be at least one NON-WEP, NON-TKIP and NON-HIDDEN Front haul BSS
per radio.

 Important Note about WPA3
 This feature can be used in MAP R2 and above MAP versions and we can configure the device to WPA3 security
 either in two modes one is WPA3 Transition mode (PSK+SAE) or in SAE only mode. According to MAP R2
 specification, if a Multi-AP Controller sends an M2 indicating Fronthaul BSS, it shall not set the Authentication
 Type attribute in that M2 to 0x0040 (SAE only). The Multi-AP Controller must not configure SAE-only mode on
 fronthaul BSSs. However, if the Agent indicates support for SAE in the M1, the Controller might configure a
 fronthaul BSS to 0x0060 (PSK+SAE), aka WPA3 Transition Mode. However, user can configure device in any WPA3
 security modes based on its requirement, but it may have interoperability issues with other vendor solutions.

Important Note about Max BSS number in the mesh network

Maximum number of BSS supported in topology: 76
This restriction is due to the size limit of combined infra metrics sent by the controller.

For example for a 3 device MAP network with each device supporting 3 radios each, BSS distribution can be as
follows:
         Controller (16 BSS on Radio1 + 8 BSS on Radio2 + 8 BSS on Radio3)
         Agent 1 (16 BSS on Radio1 + 8 BSS on Radio2 + 8 BSS on Radio3)
       Agent 2 (4 BSS on Radio1 + 4 BSS on Radio2 + 4 BSS on Radio3)

So , total BSS number in network is 76.
If BSS are more, number of MAP devices supported in the network will be less. But max number of BSS in
topology should not exceed 76. Similarly vice versa, if we need to support more devices in mesh network then
bss on some devices will have to be reduced.
Till now testing of 76 BSS has been done only with max device in mesh network supported as 3.

In MAP (inside mapd_i.h) , 1905daemon( inside p1905_database.h) and WAPP (inside mapd.h) daemons we have
a macro with the name :
 MAX_SET_BSS_INFO_NUM

This macro’s value can be tuned based on the requirement
Based on this value various buffers (especially related to the combine infra metrics response, onboarding related
BSS configuration variables) are allocated in the daemon code.

3.2.3.4       Onboarding method via Wi-Fi with out-of-band DPP bootstrapping
Following are the brief steps following during Wi-Fi DPP QR based onboarding. It is expected that controller to
have QR code of Enrollee before triggering onboarding:

        new Enrollee onboarding agent.
     • In Wi-Fi onboarding the Enrollee Agent initiate sending presence announcement frame on its channel
        list(which can be updated periodically based on CCE field from Proxy agent beacon/probe responses).
     • Proxy Agent encapsulate the DPP frames coming from Enrollee Agent into the Proxied DPP encap
        messages for controller and decapsulate the Proxied DPP messages in to the DPP frames for Enrollee
        agent.
     • After DPP authentication, the enrollee agent sends DPP configuration request with object. Upon
        receiving it the controller sends DPP config response.
     • DPP configuration response consist of 1905 connector and bsta Connector. Enrollee agent uses the BSTA
        connector to extract Backhaul BSS information for BSTA connection using AKM specified in config
        response. The 1905 connector will be used by 1905 to establish secure 1905 connection between
        devices.
     • All DPP Authentication and Configuration frames between controller and proxy agent are converted to
        1905 proxied DPP encap messages.
     • After DPP authentication and configuration and BSTA connection, the controller and Agent establish
        secure 1905 connection using 1905 peer discovery and 1905 4 way handshake.
     • After secure connection establishment, Agent sends BSS configuration request to which Controller
        sends BSS config response consist of FBSS and BBSS credentials which are to be configured on Agent.

3.2.3.4.1       DPP Presence Announcement and channel list selection procedure
 A channel list on which to send DPP Presence Announcement frames by the enrollee shall be derived
 From the following procedure:
    1. One from each of the following channels, as supported and configurable:
              a. 2.4 GHz: Channel 6 (2.437 GHz)
              b. 5 GHz: Channel 44 (5.220 GHz) if local regulations permit operation only in the 5.150 – 5.250
                  GHz band and Channel 149 (5.745 GHz) otherwise
    2. Scan all supported bands and add each channel on which an AP is advertising the Configurator
        Connectivity element to the channel list
    3. DPP chirping will be started based on priority flag present in /etc/dpp_cfg.txt or in /etc/config/mapd
        file if SKU supports UCI i.e presence_band_priority. If presence_band_priority=5g, then presence
        announcement will be started on 5G channels first then on 2G channels. EasyMesh Daemons needs to
        be restarted post this change or need to reboot the device in order to apply this change.
        In default /etc/dpp_cfg.txt, presence_band_priority will not be present so default value will be used as
        5g.




                                    Figure 3- 24. Presence band priority parameter

    4.      The Enrollee shall follow the procedure below for sending the Presence Announcement frames:
                a. For each channel in the channel list generated, the Enrollee, shall send a DPP Presence
                    Announcement frame and listen for 2 seconds to receive a DPP Authentication Request
                    frame. If a valid DPP Authentication Request frame is not received, it shall repeat the
                    presence announcement for the next channel in the channel list.
                b. When all channels in the channel list have been exhausted, the Enrollee shall pause for at
                    least 30 seconds before repeating the procedure in step a above.
                c. If the device has cycled through the procedure (Steps a & b) four times without receipt of a
                    valid DPP Authentication Request frame, it shall generate a new channel list using the steps
                    1,2 specified in this section, prior to resuming the presence announcement procedure.

    For DPP channel used in the MAP R3 controller, device Channels will be selected based on Channel planning
    not by bootstrap information.

3.2.3.9 DPP Reconfiguration
         DPP reconfiguration can be triggered in following ways:

    •    WPA2 PSK/Passphrase - A STA using a WPA2 PSK or Passphrase follows the
         standard IEEE 802.11 procedures and an unsuccessful 4-way handshake using
         the provided PSK or Passphrase may trigger reconfiguration.

    •    WPA3 Password - A STA using a WPA3 Personal password follows the SAE authentication as per the IEEE
         802.11 procedures and an unsuccessful SAE authentication may trigger reconfiguration.

    •    DPP Connector - A STA using a DPP Connector attempts the Network Introduction Protocol failure with
         error STATUS_INVALID_CONNECTOR may trigger reconfiguration.

    •    DPP Client’s Connector expiry date - After the expiry date, the information is no longer valid. Enrollee
         will compare the current time to evaluate the validity of credential, After the credential expired may
         trigger reconfiguration.
         ap_expiry parameter needs to be added for configurator in file (/etc/dpp_cfg.txt).
         For example:
         ap_expiry=2021-05-25T22:56:22 (YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS).

3.2.3.10      DPP Onboarding Important Points
This section helps share the DPP Onboarding important details:

    •    Post onboarding, connector information is saved and maintained on reboot.
    •    URI will be saved in a dpp configuration file and maintained on reboot.
    •    Addition of URI is limited to 100, after 100 it will overwrite from 1st.
    •    If DPP Onboarding Ongoing and DPP Onboarding triggered again then second dpp onboarding trigger
         will be rejected.
    •    Default Preferred onboarding method is DPP, and if set to WPS then URI will not be send.
         Preferred onboarding can be modified via API as explained in MAP R3 API section.
    •    As DPP Spec allows config for DPP/SAE/WPA2-PSK. So make sure authmode is set accordingly in WTS
         file. DPP+SAE+PSK is suggested combination to be set to cover all cases for Backhaul and for Fronthaul
         use SAE Transition mode as many Mobile STA don’t support DPP and not connect if DPP is set by AP.
    •    Make sure atleast 1 fronthaul exist as DPP Onboarding uses fronthaul. So minimum of 2 BSS is needed
         for DPP onboarding, one as Backhaul BSS and one as front haul BSS.

3.2.5         Backhaul Configuration Save
After onboarding is complete at enroller agent, the configuration of the backhaul BSS is saved in non-volatile
memory of the device.

WPS based onboarding again.

and there is no need to trigger DPP based onboarding again.

supports DPP then first DPP Network Introduction Protocol is done and then bSTA connection is formed. Also in
R3 device, 11ax capabilities is used using new WiFi6 TLV as defined in R3 spec. In R1/R2 11ax capabilities was
